knowledge_points.label: muP in practice: stabilizes scaling (CerebrasGPT), survives most modern tweaks, breaks on RMSNorm gains and strong weight decay
knowledge_points.statement: Empirically muP delivers much of what it promises: CerebrasGPT (0.1B to 13B, Chinchilla recipe) finds it makes scaling more stable, a replication confirms the optimal LR is roughly constant across widths, and it survives SwiGLU and squared-ReLU activations, large and small batches, initialization variants such as zero attention, and regularizers, but learnable RMSNorm gains break it (and can be removed with little loss), sign-based optimizers such as Lion appear to break it (said aloud; the slide only asks 'Do they transfer?'), and strong (0.1) weight decay is 'maybe the only significant muP failure', so overall muP is useful mainly because standard parametrization is quite a bit more unstable.

anchors.quote: CerebrasGPT – 0.1 to 13B models trained with the Chinchilla recipe. Core finding – using muP parametrization makes scaling more stable

Modern LMs have many components that deviate from muP's theory Activations – SwiGLU and squared relu Batch sizes – Large / small Initialization variations – zero attention, etc. RMS norm gains Exotic optimizers (Lion) Regularizers Which of these (if any) break muP?
In our arch – RMSNorm has learnable gains. This turns out to break muP But these gains can be removed with little loss of perf..
What about strong (0.1) weight decay? – this is maybe the only significant muP failure
Overall, muP generally seems useful – insofar that SP is quite a bit more unstable. Current evidence suggests that muP parametrization / initialization may be easier to tune.
Q1: Does muP work as claimed? When we scale widths, is optimal LR constant?
they have Cerebras GPT from a couple of years ago, where they were training the 0.1 to 13b models using the usual Chinchilla recipe, but also including a muP variant

if they use the muP parameterization, then their scaling law fits are generally more stable. Their projected muP trends are almost right on the money for their actual models. Whereas, I think their non-muP models fluctuated much more wildly
There's an interesting paper by an independent researcher on basically stress testing muP in lots of different ways.
that particular paper replicated a bunch of the muP results for language models trained at different scales. ... you get exactly the learning rate optimality invariance
Technically, SwiGLU does not fit into muP, neither does initialize variations, initialization or RMS norm. ... which of these things that are not allowed by the theory really break muP?

for the most part, these mostly work with muP. But some of the things that don't work is if you learn the gain term in RMS norm, this turns out to break muP. Although, these can be removed in many cases without necessarily hurting you
It also seems to break if you use more exotic optimizers like Lion, which basically rely on the sign of the gradient. And sign gradient is like a spiritually similar to muon
if you do large decoupled weight decay, you end up with significant muP failure. So this is maybe the one stress test that it does fail.

misconceptions.belief: muP is a theorem, so any model built with muP init and LR rules will have a width-independent optimal LR.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The derivation assumes a deep linear network with SGD/Adam and no extras. p53-p56 test the deviations of real LMs and find that learnable RMSNorm gains and strong weight decay break the transfer, so muP is an empirical recipe whose assumptions must be checked.

misconceptions.belief: Because muP fails under strong weight decay and RMSNorm gains, standard parametrization is the safer default.
misconceptions.why_wrong: p57: muP seems useful precisely because SP is quite a bit more unstable; the failures are fixable (remove gains) or avoidable (weaker decay), while SP's drifting optimum has no fix short of re-tuning.

transfer.q: The same team instead removes the RMSNorm gains and lowers weight decay to a small value, but switches the hidden-layer optimizer to Muon. Which slide-53 category does this fall under, what does the deck say about it, and what single experiment would settle it for them?
